mercenary

/MUR-suh-nair-ee/ - the stress falls on MUR · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Mercenary means motivated entirely by money or personal gain — willing to do, drop, or switch anything if it pays.

Her tell-all book about the scandal struck reviewers as mercenary — rushed to print for the trial's opening day and padded to justify the price.

Example

The whistle-blower's memoir insists her motives weren't mercenary — and the record backs her: she turned down the network's six-figure exclusive and gave the documents away.

Mercenary is an accusation about motive: not 'did money change hands' but 'was money the reason.' The word began as a noun — a mercenarius was a soldier fighting for wages rather than for a country — and the adjective keeps that chill: allegiance for hire.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

greedy: Greedy means wanting more and more of something than you need — food, money, attention; it measures the appetite's size, while mercenary is about what steers the choices: pay, and pay alone.

venal: Venal means open to bribery — a venal official sells the powers of an office; mercenary conduct needn't be corrupt at all, just priced: the mercenary consultant works for whoever writes the check.

self-serving: Self-serving means arranged to benefit oneself in whatever currency — credit, comfort, advancement; mercenary names the money version specifically.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

altruistic: acting for others' good at a cost to yourself

principled: guided by conviction rather than advantage

Where it sits · how completely money runs the motive

opportunistic → mercenary → venal

opportunistic vs. mercenary: Opportunistic is milder than mercenary: the opportunist grabs advantages as they float past, while the mercenary has gone further — pay has become the whole compass.

venal vs. mercenary: Venal is darker than mercenary: mercenary loyalty merely follows the highest bidder, but venality puts duties and offices themselves up for sale — the judge's ruling, the inspector's signature.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — mercen-: wages, pay, reward (Latin merces, from merx, 'goods')

Suffix — -ary: connected with; a person or thing concerned with

Put it together: Latin merx meant goods for sale, and its child merces meant the wages paid for work. Mercenarius — merces plus -arius — was the man whose sword went to whoever paid, and English kept both the noun and the adjective's cold judgment. The merx family trades on: merchant, merchandise, market all keep shop in it.

Use the root in a new word: marketable: Her adviser kept nudging the thesis toward something more marketable, and she kept nudging it back.

Word Choice

cold / accusing

Mercenary is a verdict on motive, so save it for cases where the money truly did the steering — charging for work is not mercenary; abandoning a loyalty for a better fee is. As a noun it still means a soldier for hire, and the adjective borrows that figure's chill: whatever it modifies, somewhere a flag has been traded for a paycheck.
